questions.stem:
A switch has this configuration:

username admin privilege 15 secret Str0ng!Pass
line vty 0 4
 login local

What does it do?

options.text: Remote (VTY) logins are checked against the username and password stored on the switch itself
options.rationale: Correct: 'login local' uses the switch's own account database.

options.text: Remote logins are sent to a RADIUS server for checking
options.rationale: Nothing here configures AAA or a RADIUS server.

options.text: Remote logins need only a line password, with no username
options.rationale: That would be 'login' with a line password; 'login local' requires a username.

options.text: The password is stored in cleartext because it was set with 'secret'
options.rationale: 'secret' stores a hash; it is the 'password' keyword that leaves it readable.

questions.explanation: Local authentication stores accounts on the device itself ('username ... secret ...'), and 'login local' applies them to the lines. Because each device holds its own credentials, it doesn't scale.
questions.discriminator_tested: Local authentication keeps credentials on each device; 'secret' is hashed.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the steps of the iAAA model?

options.text: Identification, authentication, authorization, accounting
options.rationale: Correct: who are you, prove it, what may you do, what did you do.

options.text: Authentication, identification, accounting, authorization
options.rationale: You must claim an identity before proving it, and accounting comes last.

options.text: Identification, authorization, authentication, accounting
options.rationale: Permissions can't be decided before identity is proven.

options.text: Accounting, identification, authentication, authorization
options.rationale: Accounting records what happened, so it comes last.

questions.explanation: The iAAA model runs identification (who are you?), authentication (prove it), authorization (what may you do?), then accounting (what did you do?).
questions.discriminator_tested: Who are you? Prove it. What may you do? What did you do?

questions.stem: A user enters a username and the correct password and passes the login check. What has been established at this point?

options.text: Their identity has been authenticated; nothing yet determines what they may access
options.rationale: Correct: authentication proves identity only.

options.text: They are authorized to use every resource on the network
options.rationale: Permissions are decided separately, by authorization.

options.text: Accounting for the session is complete
options.rationale: Accounting records activity over the session; it is not finished at login.

options.text: They have completed multifactor authentication
options.rationale: A password is a single factor.

questions.explanation: Authentication verifies a claimed identity using one or more factors (something you know, have, or are). It proves who you are but says nothing yet about permissions.
questions.discriminator_tested: Authentication proves identity; it does not grant permissions.

questions.stem: Which two login methods count as MFA? (Choose two.)

options.text: A password plus a code from a hardware token
options.rationale: Correct: something you know plus something you have.

options.text: A smart card plus a PIN
options.rationale: Correct: something you have plus something you know.

options.text: A password plus a second, different password
options.rationale: Both are something you know, so it is one category.

options.text: A password plus the answer to a security question
options.rationale: Both are something you know.

options.text: A fingerprint plus a face scan
options.rationale: Both are something you are, so it is one category.

questions.explanation: MFA requires two or more different factor categories: something you know, have, or are. Two items from the same category, such as two passwords, are not MFA.
questions.discriminator_tested: MFA needs different factor categories; two of the same kind is not MFA.

questions.stem: A company is choosing a second factor for remote access. Which MFA method is generally strongest against interception and redirection?

options.text: A time-based code from an authenticator app or hardware token
options.rationale: Correct: the code is generated on the device and isn't sent over a channel an attacker can redirect.

options.text: A code sent by SMS
options.rationale: SMS codes can be intercepted or redirected, for example through SIM swapping.

options.text: A code read out in an automated voice call
options.rationale: Voice calls can be redirected through call forwarding or a hijacked number.

options.text: A code sent by email
options.rationale: An emailed code is only as safe as the email account.

questions.explanation: Common MFA methods include email, SMS, voice call, and time-based hardware or software tokens. Time-based tokens are generally stronger; codes sent by SMS, voice, or email can be intercepted or redirected.
questions.discriminator_tested: Time-based tokens are stronger; SMS, voice, and email codes can be intercepted.

questions.stem: An employee logs in successfully but gets 'Access denied' when opening the payroll folder. Which iAAA function denied the request?

options.text: Authorization
options.rationale: Correct: it decides what an authenticated user may access.

options.text: Authentication
options.rationale: Authentication succeeded; the login worked.

options.text: Accounting
options.rationale: Accounting records activity; it doesn't allow or deny anything.

options.text: Identification
options.rationale: The employee's identity was already claimed and proven.

questions.explanation: Authorization determines what an authenticated user may access or do, and it happens after authentication. Here, identity was proven, but the permission was refused.
questions.discriminator_tested: Authorization happens after authentication and decides access.

questions.stem: How does identity and access management (IAM) relate to AAA?

options.text: IAM is the umbrella program that manages identities and their access across their whole lifecycle; AAA is one mechanism inside it
options.rationale: Correct: IAM covers joining, changing roles, and leaving; AAA enforces access at login and use.

options.text: They are two names for the same thing
options.rationale: IAM is broader than the authentication, authorization, and accounting mechanisms.

options.text: AAA is the umbrella program; IAM is a protocol inside it
options.rationale: This reverses the relationship.

options.text: IAM is a newer protocol that replaces RADIUS
options.rationale: IAM is a set of processes and tools, not a network protocol.

questions.explanation: Identity and access management is the set of processes and tools that manage identities and their access throughout their lifecycle. AAA is one mechanism within that program.
questions.discriminator_tested: IAM is the umbrella program; AAA is one mechanism inside it.

questions.stem: A marketing intern's account was given domain administrator rights 'to avoid permission tickets.' Later, malware on the intern's laptop runs with the intern's rights. Which principle was violated, and what was the consequence?

options.text: Least privilege; the malware inherited administrator rights and could do far more damage
options.rationale: Correct: the account had much more access than the job needed.

options.text: Defense in depth; the network had only one firewall
options.rationale: Layering is a separate principle; the problem described is excess rights on one account.

options.text: Accounting; no logs were kept
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario concerns logging.

options.text: MFA; the intern used only a password
options.rationale: MFA protects the login; it does not limit what malware running as the user can do.

questions.explanation: Least privilege grants only the access needed for the job. It limits the damage from mistakes, malware, and insiders, because anything running as the user gets only the user's rights.
questions.discriminator_tested: Least privilege limits damage from mistakes, malware, and insiders.

questions.stem: A hospital has 300 nurses whose access changes whenever their duties change. Administrators want to assign permissions once to a 'Nurse' group and then simply add or remove people. Which access model is this?

options.text: RBAC (role-based access control)
options.rationale: Correct: permissions attach to the role, and people get access through it.

options.text: Assigning permissions to each individual user
options.rationale: That is the opposite of what the administrators want.

options.text: Least privilege
options.rationale: Least privilege is a principle about how much access to give, not a way of assigning it.

options.text: Accounting
options.rationale: Accounting records activity; it doesn't assign permissions.

questions.explanation: In RBAC, permissions attach to roles and users get access through their role, rather than through permissions assigned to each individual.
questions.discriminator_tested: RBAC: permissions attach to roles, not individuals.

questions.stem: After an outage, investigators need to know which administrator ran the command that changed the core switch's routing, and when. Which iAAA function provides this?

options.text: Accounting
options.rationale: Correct: it records who did what and when.

options.text: Authentication
options.rationale: Authentication proved who logged in, but it doesn't record their commands.

options.text: Authorization
options.rationale: Authorization decided whether the command was allowed; it doesn't keep a history.

options.text: Identification
options.rationale: Identification is the initial identity claim.

questions.explanation: Accounting records who did what and when, such as logins, commands, and session data. It is the after-the-fact audit trail that makes actions traceable.
questions.discriminator_tested: Accounting is the after-the-fact audit trail.

questions.stem: A firewall log shows a wireless controller sending authentication requests to a server on UDP 1812 and accounting records on UDP 1813. Which protocol is this?

options.text: RADIUS
options.rationale: Correct: RADIUS uses UDP 1812 for authentication and 1813 for accounting.

options.text: TACACS+
options.rationale: TACACS+ uses TCP 49.

options.text: SNMP
options.rationale: SNMP uses UDP 161 and 162 for device monitoring.

options.text: TFTP
options.rationale: TFTP uses UDP 69 for file transfer.

questions.explanation: RADIUS is centralized AAA over UDP (1812 for authentication, 1813 for accounting). It is an open standard, typical for network access such as 802.1X, Wi-Fi, and VPN.
questions.discriminator_tested: RADIUS: UDP 1812/1813, typical for network access.

questions.stem: A network team wants a central AAA server for administrators logging in to routers and switches. They want each command authorized separately and the whole session payload encrypted. Which protocol fits?

options.text: TACACS+
options.rationale: Correct: it separates authentication, authorization, and accounting, and it encrypts the entire payload.

options.text: RADIUS
options.rationale: RADIUS combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password.

options.text: Local authentication
options.rationale: Local accounts aren't central and don't scale across many devices.

options.text: SNMPv3
options.rationale: SNMPv3 secures device monitoring; it isn't an AAA protocol.

questions.explanation: TACACS+ is centralized AAA over TCP 49 that encrypts the entire payload and separates authentication, authorization, and accounting. That makes it typical for device administration.
questions.discriminator_tested: TACACS+: TCP 49, full encryption, separate A/A/A; for device administration.

questions.stem:
A router has the login method list:

aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local

An administrator mistypes their password, and the TACACS+ server rejects it. What happens next?

options.text: The login fails; the local account is tried only when the TACACS+ server can't be reached
options.rationale: Correct: a rejection is a final answer, not a reason to fall back.

options.text: The router falls back to its local account and checks the password again
options.rationale: Fallback happens only when the server is unreachable.

options.text: The administrator is logged in with limited privileges
options.rationale: A rejected login gets no access at all.

options.text: The router disables AAA until it is rebooted
options.rationale: A rejected login doesn't change the AAA configuration.

questions.explanation: Configuring iAAA means enabling AAA, defining the server, and building method lists applied to lines. The order in a method list matters, and the next method is used only when a server is unreachable, not when it rejects the user.
questions.discriminator_tested: Fallback to local happens on server unreachable, not on reject.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes a RADIUS login on a wireless network?

options.text: The user enters credentials; the access point sends an Access-Request to the RADIUS server; the server answers Access-Accept, Access-Reject, or Access-Challenge; the access point acts on the answer
options.rationale: Correct: the access device is the RADIUS client.

options.text: The user's laptop sends an Access-Request straight to the RADIUS server, which then tells the access point
options.rationale: The user's endpoint is not the RADIUS client; the access device is.

options.text: The RADIUS server sends Access-Accept first, and then the user enters credentials
options.rationale: The server can't accept credentials it hasn't received.

options.text: The access point sends Access-Accept to the RADIUS server
options.rationale: Accept, Reject, and Challenge come from the server, not the access device.

questions.explanation: In the RADIUS login process, credentials go to the access device (switch or access point), which sends an Access-Request to the RADIUS server and acts on the Accept, Reject, or Challenge it gets back.
questions.discriminator_tested: The access device is the RADIUS client, not the user's endpoint.

questions.stem: Which change to the password policy adds the most resistance to guessing?

options.text: Raising the minimum length from 8 to 16 characters
options.rationale: Correct: each added character multiplies the number of possible passwords.

options.text: Requiring one symbol in an 8-character password
options.rationale: Complexity alone adds less strength than length, and users tend to add symbols predictably.

options.text: Forcing a password change every 30 days
options.rationale: Frequent changes don't make each password harder to guess.

options.text: Allowing users to reuse their previous password
options.rationale: Reuse weakens the policy.

questions.explanation: Longer passwords with mixed character types resist guessing, but password length adds more strength than complexity alone.
questions.discriminator_tested: Length adds more strength than complexity alone.

questions.stem: A strict policy now locks any account after three failed attempts. Every morning, an attacker deliberately enters wrong passwords for every executive's account. What is the attacker achieving?

options.text: Abusing the password lockout to keep the executives out of their own accounts
options.rationale: Correct: lockout can itself be used as a denial-of-service tool.

options.text: Nothing harmful, because lockout stops the brute force attempt
options.rationale: The guessing is stopped, but the legitimate users are locked out every day.

options.text: Cracking the executives' passwords through the lockout
options.rationale: Locked accounts can't be guessed further.

options.text: Disabling the accounting logs
options.rationale: Failed attempts are logged; nothing here affects accounting.

questions.explanation: Password lockout locks an account after a set number of failed attempts, which counters online brute force. The same mechanism can be abused to lock out legitimate users.
questions.discriminator_tested: Lockout counters online brute force but can be abused to lock out legitimate users.

questions.stem: A PC is plugged into a switch port configured for 802.1X but has not authenticated yet. By default, what traffic can it send through the port?

options.text: Only authentication traffic, until it authenticates successfully
options.rationale: Correct: the port stays blocked for everything else until success.

options.text: All traffic, because 802.1X only logs connections
options.rationale: 802.1X enforces access; it doesn't just log.

options.text: Only web traffic to the internet
options.rationale: Nothing but authentication traffic passes before success.

options.text: Nothing at all, not even authentication traffic
options.rationale: Then the device could never authenticate.

questions.explanation: 802.1X is port-based access control: a port passes only authentication traffic until the device authenticates, and stays blocked for everything else until then.
questions.discriminator_tested: 802.1X keeps the port blocked until authentication succeeds.

questions.stem: Which pair of 802.1X components correctly identifies who enforces the access decision at the port and who makes that decision?

options.text: The switch (authenticator) enforces; the RADIUS server (authentication server) decides
options.rationale: Correct: the authenticator enforces and the server decides.

options.text: The client (supplicant) enforces; the switch decides
options.rationale: The supplicant is the device asking for access.

options.text: The RADIUS server enforces; the supplicant decides
options.rationale: The device asking for access can't decide its own access.

options.text: The switch both enforces and decides, with no server
options.rationale: In 802.1X the decision comes from the authentication server.

questions.explanation: 802.1X components: the supplicant is the client, the authenticator is the switch or WAP, and the authentication server is RADIUS. The authenticator enforces; the server decides.
questions.discriminator_tested: The authenticator enforces; the authentication server decides.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes the NAC process?

options.text: The device connects; it is identified and assessed; policy then sets its access level (full, restricted, quarantine, or deny)
options.rationale: Correct: identify and assess first, then apply policy.

options.text: The device gets full access first and is assessed later if problems appear
options.rationale: NAC checks before granting access.

options.text: The device is denied, then identified, then granted access whatever the result
options.rationale: Access depends on the result of the checks.

options.text: The device is assessed only after the user logs out
options.rationale: Assessment happens at or during connection.

questions.explanation: In the NAC process, a device connects, is identified and assessed, and then policy sets its access level. The outcome is policy-driven and need not be all-or-nothing.
questions.discriminator_tested: NAC outcome is policy-driven and need not be all-or-nothing.

questions.stem: A hospital's NAC system must recognize infusion pumps and printers, which can't run 802.1X client software, and place each kind in the right network segment. Which NAC capability identifies what each device is?

options.text: Profiling
options.rationale: Correct: it identifies a device's type or class from observed attributes.

options.text: Posturing
options.rationale: Posturing checks a device's health, not what kind of device it is.

options.text: A captive portal
options.rationale: A portal needs a person at a browser, which pumps and printers don't have.

options.text: Accounting
options.rationale: Accounting records activity; it doesn't identify device types.

questions.explanation: Profiling identifies what a device is (its type or class) from observed attributes. It is especially useful for devices that can't run a supplicant, such as printers and IoT devices.
questions.discriminator_tested: Profiling identifies device type; useful when a device can't run a supplicant.

questions.stem: Which two checks are examples of posturing (posture assessment)? (Choose two.)

options.text: Is the antivirus running with current definitions?
options.rationale: Correct: a device health check.

options.text: Are the latest operating system patches installed?
options.rationale: Correct: a compliance check.

options.text: Is this device a printer, a phone, or a PC?
options.rationale: Working out the device type is profiling.

options.text: Who is the user logging in?
options.rationale: Proving the user's identity is authentication.

options.text: Which network segments does this user's role allow?
options.rationale: Deciding permitted access is authorization.

questions.explanation: Posturing checks a device's health and compliance, such as patches, antivirus, and configuration. That is different from identity (authentication) and from device type (profiling).
questions.discriminator_tested: Posturing checks health, not identity or device type.

questions.stem: Why does BYOD need NAC, posture checks, and segmentation more than company-owned laptops do?

options.text: Personal devices are unmanaged and varied, so their patch level and configuration can't be assumed
options.rationale: Correct: the organization didn't set up these devices.

options.text: Personal devices can't connect to Wi-Fi without these controls
options.rationale: They can connect; the controls exist to manage the risk.

options.text: Personal devices are always infected
options.rationale: They aren't always infected; their state is simply unknown.

options.text: BYOD devices don't need any extra controls
options.rationale: Their unmanaged state is exactly why they do.

questions.explanation: BYOD means personally owned devices accessing organizational resources. Because they are unmanaged and varied, they need NAC, posture checks, and segmentation.
questions.discriminator_tested: BYOD devices are unmanaged and varied.

questions.stem: A conference center offers Wi-Fi to visitors. One visitor's infected laptop starts scanning for other devices to attack. Which design keeps that scan away from the center's internal systems?

options.text: Guest network isolation: a separate segment with internet-only access and no route to internal resources
options.rationale: Correct: the scan can't reach what the segment can't route to.

options.text: Visitors and staff on the same network, with a captive portal for visitors
options.rationale: A portal controls who gets on, but visitors would still share the internal network.

options.text: WPA3-Personal on a network shared by staff and visitors
options.rationale: Encryption protects traffic in the air; it doesn't separate visitors from internal systems.

options.text: Device profiling for every visitor
options.rationale: Profiling identifies device types; on its own it doesn't isolate them.

questions.explanation: Guest network isolation places guests on a separate segment with internet-only access, isolated from internal resources. Isolation is the control that contains a compromised guest device.
questions.discriminator_tested: Guest isolation separates guests from internal resources.

questions.stem: A hotel's open Wi-Fi shows a login page asking for a room number and surname before any browsing works. A guest assumes that once logged in, their wireless traffic is encrypted. Is the guest right?

options.text: No: the captive portal is only a gate for getting on the network; it doesn't encrypt wireless traffic
options.rationale: Correct: an open network stays unencrypted after the portal login.

options.text: Yes: logging in through the portal turns on WPA3
options.rationale: A portal doesn't change the wireless security mode.

options.text: Yes: if the login page uses HTTPS, all later traffic is encrypted too
options.rationale: HTTPS protects only that page's connection, not the rest of the guest's traffic.

options.text: No: captive portals only work on wired networks
options.rationale: Captive portals are common on wireless networks.

questions.explanation: A captive portal intercepts a new user's first web request and requires a login or acceptance before granting access. It is a gate for guest and BYOD onboarding, not encryption of wireless traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: A captive portal is an onboarding gate, not encryption.
